cim: Autonomous Mind | Congress scrambles to keep pace with AI
cim_eredeti: Autonomous Mind | Congress scrambles to keep pace with AI
szoveg_eredeti:
Editor’s note: Artificial intelligence is advancing at a pace that lawmakers, regulators and even some of its creators struggle to keep up. While Congress debates oversight frameworks and ethical standards, leading technology companies are deploying increasingly powerful systems capable of learning, adapting and improving with minimal human intervention. This series examines the growing divide between the speed of innovation and the pace of governance, exploring the risks, opportunities and unanswered questions surrounding a technology that is rapidly becoming embedded in every aspect of modern life.

Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than lawmakers can regulate it, raising a question Congress can no longer avoid: Can the United States protect Americans from AI risks without slowing the technology and risking China taking the lead?

Colorado’s congressional delegation is largely united on one point — artificial intelligence needs guardrails.

They, however, differ on how those guardrails should work, how much government oversight is necessary and how to balance regulation with the national security and economic imperative of keeping America ahead of rival nations, particularly China.

The debate has grown more urgent as AI companies develop increasingly powerful systems and technology that, experts warn, government oversight is struggling to keep pace.

Some had drawn parallels to the nuclear weapons race.

“It’s very important to point out that nuclear weapons certainly are an existential threat,” said Steve Beaty, an MSU Denver professor of computer science who has worked in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity since the 1990s. “But the way we worked through that was in collaboration with Russia.”

Beaty said AI presents a different challenge because the technology is advancing so quickly.

“We’ve never had a technology quite like this,” he said. “That is on par with human intelligence and is evolving very rapidly.”

That acceleration is at the center of worries from both Democrats and Republicans alike in Colorado’s delegation, though they also see the technology’s potential and worry about ceding the race to other nations with antagonistic views toward the U.S.

Democratic U.S. Rep. Brittany Pettersen, who served on a bipartisan congressional AI task force, said Congress has failed to respond with the urgency the technology requires.

“It is moving quicker than we have,” Pettersen said. “We haven’t done anything to address this at the federal level. So, it’s unacceptable.”

Pettersen said Congress should establish independent audits of AI systems, require companies to report significant incidents and create a federal regulatory structure with the resources and technical expertise necessary to oversee the technology.

“We need to have oversight of AI technologies,” she said. “We need to have independent audits. We need to ensure that the technologies that they’re releasing are not a danger to our country.”

Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans also argued that Congress needs to establish guardrails, but he places greater emphasis on ensuring that regulation does not cause America to surrender its technological edge to China.

Evans said the U.S. must lead AI development to influence how the technology is used.

“Two things can be true at once,” Evans said. “The United States has to lead in this space … but we have to have common-sense guardrails around it, too.”

The technology at the center of the debate has changed dramatically since the early days of artificial intelligence.

Beaty said researchers understood how to train neural networks decades ago but lacked the computing power necessary to make them broadly useful.

That changed as graphics processing units, or GPUs, became capable of handling enormous amounts of computation.

Beaty said a major turning point came in 2017 with the publication of the research paper “Attention Is All You Need,” which introduced the transformer architecture that became foundational to modern large language models.

Since then, AI systems have grown increasingly capable of generating text, writing software, analyzing information, producing images and performing tasks that once required human judgment.

The technology is also beginning to move toward systems that can modify or improve aspects of their own software.

Beaty described the emerging process as “recursive self-improvement.”

Rather than humans writing every improvement into an AI system, researchers can ask an AI system to determine how it could become more capable and generate software to make those changes.

However, Beaty cautioned against interpreting that development as evidence that AI has become conscious or will inevitably turn against humans.

But, he said, it does create a new challenge for regulators.

“Now it is, if you will, learning, self-learning, which it hasn’t done up to this point,” Beaty said.

The speed of those changes makes traditional regulation particularly difficult.

Social media companies, such as Meta, took years to face comprehensive government scrutiny. By contrast, AI capabilities can change substantially between congressional hearings.

“We’re not going to have four years here,” Beaty said.

Pettersen said Congress needs to establish a regulatory system that can evaluate AI before systems are widely deployed.

She pointed to several areas where she believes Congress should act, including independent testing, transparency requirements and an agency with enough funding and technical expertise to oversee the industry.

Pettersen also said the federal government needs to require companies to identify unintended consequences and report negative findings from internal testing.

“It’s absolutely possible to take on as long as we have the right leadership and willingness to do so,” she said. “And it couldn’t be more urgent.”

Pettersen said Republicans and Democrats had worked together on an earlier congressional task force focused on AI. She accused U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and President Donald Trump of failing to prioritize the issue.

After a recent meeting with Johnson and top AI executives, Trump appointed Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence and to lead a new federal AI task force. The task force will coordinate the federal effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a post on social media.

Republicans argued that Congress has demonstrated that bipartisan legislation is possible.

Evans pointed to legislation he has worked on involving AI chatbots, open-source AI and the massive data centers required to power AI systems.

One of those measures, the Ratepayer Protection Act, passed the House 417-3 before the Senate blocked it, with votes from Colorado Sens. John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennett playing a key role in killing the legislation.

The bill had sought to address the electricity and infrastructure demands created by large data centers, aiming to prevent those costs from shifting to other electricity customers.

Evans said the legislation illustrates the broader challenge facing lawmakers: AI policy increasingly touches energy, privacy, national security, jobs and the economy.

The debate over regulation becomes more complicated because China is simultaneously racing to expand its own AI capabilities.

Evans said allowing China to become the dominant AI power would leave Americans with less influence over how the technology develops.

He compared the situation to the Cold War space race.

“Technology has no conscience of its own,” Evans said, recalling former President John F. Kennedy’s argument that technology ultimately reflects the values of the people controlling it.
